writing.exampleCaption: Complete std-only matrix-binary-search program for its typed teaching fixture. Parsing and output construction are separate from the core algorithm.
writing.explanation:
Treat the 3×4 sample as a single sorted array of length 12. Flat index i maps to row i/4 and column i%4. Search for 16 returns true; individually sorted rows without global row-major order would not suffice.

The worked program is a complete executable for this pattern. Its core function uses typed input so the state transitions remain visible. The challenge input contract is: Return true when 16 is present. The visible fixture is `[[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]]` and its example result is `true`. The implementation and additional semantic fixtures were checked against an independent reference calculation. Those bounded tests establish these examples; they are not a proof for all inputs or a measurement on an iPhone.

Return a canonical String from solve: lowercase true/false for booleans; decimal integers without extra signs, leading zeros or whitespace; comma-separated sequence values and semicolon-separated groups. Whole-number medians have no decimal suffix; half medians use .5. Do not append a newline to the returned value. Preserve the explicitly named textual sentinels such as none or #. Input fixtures are bounded so the demonstrated arithmetic fits its named Rust types; satisfy the stated input preconditions before applying the algorithm.

String and character-grid fixtures use ASCII unless the lesson explicitly specifies Unicode scalar values.

Begin with the concrete question: Return true when 16 is present. For the visible input `[[1,3,5,7],[10,11,16,20],[23,30,34,60]]`, the stated result is `true`. Before reading code, name the smallest piece of information that must survive from one step to the next. Binary search maintains an interval that is still capable of containing the answer. State precisely why the discarded half cannot contain it. That is the mental model for Flattened Matrix Search; it gives you a reason for each update instead of a line of code to memorise.

The core mechanism is this: Map a flat midpoint back to row and column when rows form one global sorted order. Treat it as a claim to test after every operation. Write down the state before the first operation, update it once, and ask which part of the claim is still true. If an item is skipped, inserted, or removed, explain why that action cannot destroy an answer that should be retained. A useful trace has columns for the current input position, the state before the step, the action, and the state afterward. Use the visible sample until the expected result becomes inevitable rather than merely plausible.

Finally justify the stated bound, O(log(rows*cols)) time · O(1) space. Count how often an item, edge, state, or candidate can enter the main operation; do not infer the bound from the number of loop keywords alone. Check no match, duplicate matches, the first and last valid positions, and an answer at the boundary of the search domain. Predict the result for a smallest legal input and for one case that stresses the invariant. If your prediction disagrees with a hand trace, repair the state definition before changing code.
